title: Урок игры на рояле  (The Piano Lesson)

segments.t: Restaurant owner Dmitry Nagiyev calls young cook and musician Denis over to the grand piano in the dining room. Nagiyev has a romantic date with a professional pianist in two days and demands that Denis teach him to play like a virtuoso immediately. Let's listen to Nagiyev's ultimatum in Russian.
У меня свидание с одной пианисткой.
А у тебя просто выбора нет.
Let's break down Nagiyev's piano request and Denis's response line by line.
'Dmitry Vladimirovich, did you call for me?' Denis addresses the restaurant owner respectfully with a plural past-tense verb.
'I adore all this music.' Nagiyev gestures at the grand piano using an expressive first-person present verb meaning to adore.
'Only I do not know how to play at all.' In Russian, a dedicated modal verb expresses knowing how to perform a learned skill.
'I used to know how, but I already forgot.' Notice how Russian puts 'earlier' and 'to forget' together in a short, direct phrase where word endings show how the ideas connect.
'Can you teach me quickly?' In spoken Russian, the words stay in their normal statement order and Nagiyev's rising voice at the end turns the line into a question.
'Well, theoretically in about four months.' Placing the noun for month before the preposition expresses an approximate four-month time period.
'I need it by the evening after tomorrow.' Nagiyev demands an impossible deadline using a single compound temporal adverb for the day after tomorrow.
У меня свидание с одной пианисткой.
'I have a date with a certain pianist.' Russians say 'by me' or 'with us' where English says 'I have' or 'we have', without needing a separate word for 'have'.
'Maybe you should hire a tutor instead?' In spoken Russian, the words stay in their normal statement order and Denis's rising voice at the end turns the line into a question.
А у тебя просто выбора нет.
'Well, you simply have no choice.' Russians say 'by me' or 'with us' where English says 'I have' or 'we have', without needing a separate word for 'have'.
'Either you will teach me right now.' Nagiyev issues an ultimatum starting with a disjunctive conjunction meaning either.
'All right, I already caught the scale.' Denis surrenders immediately using a colloquial past verb meaning to grasp the tune. Let's hear their conversation by the piano again without interruption.
У меня свидание с одной пианисткой.
А у тебя просто выбора нет.

Left with the choice of teaching Nagiyev the piano or sweeping the train station, Denis immediately sits down at the keys. Notice how Russian expresses 'either' with a disjunctive conjunction. See you next time!
